A fair friend of ours, who is all charity and benevolence, said to us the other day, "Pray tell me why YOU don't say something in favor of the Greeks." There was such a good-natured smile accompanying her countenance, that we could not for the souls of us, refuse to give her the reasons which had induced us to be silent on the subject of the persecuted Greeks, and frankly told her, that she had been lent because we are not aware, that we could do them any good but, assured her, that on some future occasion, we would lift our voices in their behalf: and we now pledge ourselves that our promise shall certainly be made GOOD.

We would gladly do so, and thus satisfy our conscience, love, and the principles of Christianity and justice. We would lend the resources that are now needed in its country to relieve Greece of her persecutions: the Greeks are worthy of all commendation, as are they who are engaged in such a display of correctness of feelings, and charity of heart, which speaks volumes in their favor.

But we must be careful, and in speaking we shall be allowed the same liberty of speech, that others enjoy; and thus far indeed we will avow, that it is our genuine opinion, that the labors of Christian America, in favor of Greek emancipation, will not be productive of any good consequences so long as to contend in all over the powers of Europe, and have encountered a common and vigorous effort to pass down Ottoman tyranny and despotism. At the present moment, Europe does not see fit to go, and it is but too apparent that as well as England and France, we must keep an eye on the powers of the earth, to make them to join in a desperate effort for the establishment of Greece. They are ALREADY and willing to enter the combat, provided they can be assured, that when the war is terminated, each shall possess the conquered and secured territory; and unless they are assured of peace and security, they will not wage war against the such power of the universe; and we must be aided by the assistance of some sums of money to aid.

bald Stuart of Augusta.

Brooke, president of the Court of Appeals was
unanimously appointed President of the Convention.

unanimously appointed Secretary of the Conven-
tion.

knowledgements for the honor you have conferred on
me—in terms corresponding possible with the feel-
ings with which it has filled me, and to address you

to your deliberations; but the indisposition under

would have been more agreeable to me therefore if
some other gentlemen had been selected much more
competent in every respect to discharge the duties
assigned me, and certainly should have declined the
duties formed when I came here to shrink from no duty
